slides.headline: The largest fish on Earth eats plankton.
slides.sub: Some of its prey is as small as 1 mm

slides.label: average length of whale sharks studied, at about 14 tonnes
slides.body: Some reportedly reach 18 m. Despite their size, whale sharks pose no danger to people. (Pictured: a snorkeller at Ningaloo Reef, Australia.)

slides.headline: It swims with its mouth open
slides.body: Seawater pours in and out through the gill slits. Mesh-like tissue acts as a sieve, trapping plankton until the shark closes its mouth to swallow.

slides.headline: A sieve with a 1 mm mesh
slides.body: Five sets of porous filter pads line each side of its throat, letting it sift out prey as small as 1 mm.

slides.headline: 300 rows of teeth it doesn't use
slides.body: Its huge mouth holds more than 300 rows of small teeth in each jaw. Scientists consider them vestigial: they play no role in feeding.

slides.headline: A gentle giant in trouble
slides.body: The IUCN Red List assessed the whale shark as Endangered in 2016. Its population is decreasing.

caption:
The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is the largest fish alive, and it feeds by straining plankton from the sea.

It swims with its mouth open and lets its gills do the sieving, catching prey as small as 1 mm. Plankton is not the whole menu: whale sharks also take sardines, anchovies, mackerels, squid and even small tuna. Sometimes one feeds hanging tail down, bobbing at the surface so water and food flood into its mouth.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.
